title: The poets
hook: the surah's name, and the poets excepted who believe, do good and remember Allah (26:224–227)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lowered wing, and your line was lower the wing. Did you listen all the way to the end before answering? Day five hundred nineteen.

In the Arabia the Prophet grew up in, the old histories describe the poet as no quiet figure with a notebook. A poet could be a weapon and a newspaper at once. A tribe's poet praised his own people and mocked their rivals, and a sharp line in verse could travel from camp to camp and stick to a family's name. So when the Prophet began reciting the Qur'an, some of his opponents had a label ready. He's just a poet. Surah Ash-Shu'ara, named for the poets, ends by answering that.

The last verses of the surah describe the poets of that time without much sympathy. Those who go astray follow them. They wander in every valley, as the image goes, chasing any mood or theme, and they say what they don't do. Commentators read this as the answer to the label: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, they say, was not wandering, and did what he said. The Qur'an says plainly elsewhere that it is not the word of a poet. But then comes a turn, an exception, in the very last verse. Except those who believe, and do good works, and remember God much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. So the surah doesn't ban poetry. It sorts it. Words that wander, and words that remember. The exception had faces. The Prophet had poets among his companions, Hassan ibn Thabit among them. A report in Bukhari says the Prophet asked Hassan to answer the Quraysh's satires in verse, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit, which Muslims understand as the angel Jibril. Another hadith in Bukhari says that some poetry is wisdom. Later, a poet named Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, who had written against the Prophet, came to him and recited a famous ode, and tradition says the Prophet gave him his own cloak. Scholars discuss the strength of that story's chains. From those beginnings grew a long tradition of praise poems for the Prophet, in Arabic and in many other languages, sung at weddings and gatherings. The test the surah gives is simple. Do the words remember God, and do the people saying them live them?
screen: `THEY WANDER IN EVERY VALLEY.` · `EXCEPT THOSE WHO BELIEVE AND REMEMBER.` · `HASSAN IBN THABIT ANSWERS IN VERSE.` · `WORDS THAT WANDER, WORDS THAT REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one devotional poem. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you know one by heart, a line of a nasheed, a verse someone once sang to you, a praise poem from your own language, let it play slowly in your mind. If you don't, decide which one you'll look up today: an Arabic ode, a Persian or Urdu poem, anything written to remember God. Notice what the words do to your breathing. Notice which line you'd want to keep. If you pray, you can say that line as a prayer. The bell holds the time.
The poets. Ash-Shu'ara, the surah named for them, which turns away the poets who wander and keeps the ones who believe, do good and remember God much. Today's word.
Your line: words that remember. Today, send one line of good poetry, or one line of praise, to someone who could use it. Day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims across the world sing and recite devotional poetry, from Arabic odes praising the Prophet to nasheeds and qawwali, while scholars hold that the Qur'an itself is not poetry.

fork.setup: the Quraysh are mocking the Prophet in verse, and the poems are spreading. you're Hassan ibn Thabit. what does the Prophet ask you to do?
options: find the poets and fight them.
fork.reveal: a report in Bukhari says he asked Hassan to answer them, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit.

original.note: Arabic: the poets; the singular, sha'ir, is tied in the lexicons to a root of perceiving.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah against poets.
what it means: a surah that answers 'he's just a poet', and then sorts words into those that wander and those that remember.
what a scholar hears: 26:224–227, the closing exception, and the hadith of Hassan ibn Thabit supported by the Holy Spirit in Bukhari, with 'some poetry is wisdom' beside it.

sources.ref: Qur'an 69:41 (not the word of a poet)

notes: All Qur'an and hadith paraphrased. Bukhari numbers (3212 for Hassan, 6145 for 'some poetry is wisdom') cited from memory; confirm.
The Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) understood as Jibril: standard Sunni reading; confirm.
Ka'b ibn Zuhayr's cloak (burda): presented as tradition with debated chains; confirm.
Original note: sha'ir from sh-'-r, to perceive/know (cf. lexicons); confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's unsourced history (seventh-century date, press offices, 'for generations') softened to what the old histories describe; narrator's claim about the Prophet attributed to commentators; 'the best known' superlative cut; the language list and Mawlid line generalized; grandmother assumption removed.
